Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette: Rizal, forty, of South Eastern Asian descent, worked as a journalist, and when the men took him, the detention facility was stark, but it was the sounds that anchored the worst of his ordeal. He had come to believe that the children crying beyond the compound walls were not merely ambient noise but a signal that he was being shifted toward the next phase. When the guards called out to one another, he would catch specific names, names he later realized mirrored the men who held him, and each one sent a quiet jolt through him. He felt the dizziness return, not as a passing spell but as a physical echo of the rough floor and the weight on his shoulders, a lightheadedness that made the edges of the room tilt. He watched the faces of those around him, searching for the flicker of intent in their eyes, certain that a shift in posture meant another strike, another question. What frightened him most was not just the pain, but the sensation that he had broken in ways others could see. He walked into rooms carrying a quiet weight, certain that anyone looking closely could read his history in his posture. Back in the city, where he spent his days in a glass-walled newsroom editing drafts and attending editorial meetings, the world moved at a pace that felt increasingly separate from his own. The noise of the office, phones ringing, keyboards clacking, a reporter laughing too loudly, made him jump. He would straighten in his chair, his pulse quickening, before realizing it was only a colleague asking for a second opinion. At lunch, the restaurant’s high chairs would sometimes catch his attention, and when a child in the corner began to cry, his stomach would tighten. He found himself ordering black coffee and skipping the food. The undereating coexisted with the avoidance of pre-event contacts, both settling into his days without pushing or pulling one another. His ex-wife had noticed the habit first, then his closest colleagues from the years before the event. When he saw them, he would cross the street or wait for them to pass, telling himself it was simply convenience, though the truth was closer to a need to stay clear of the people who still carried the unmarked version of him. He spent hours at his desk staring at the bylines on his articles, his mind circling the same questions: if he had spoken when the older man did, if he had stood instead of kneeling, if he had refused the water, would the days have folded differently? The prevention rumination settled into his routine like a second job, heavy and unyielding. The negative emotions accumulated in quiet waves. Guilt and shame followed him into the subway; anger flared when a deadline was pushed too hard. He did not feel that these emotions drove one another, but that they lived together in him, each occupying its own space. He felt defective in a way that had nothing to do with his work and everything to do with his nature. He had valued composure, yet during the longest nights in captivity, he had begged, he had screamed, he had acted in ways that felt like betrayals of his own code. Now, even in the safety of his apartment, he watched the people on his street, their hands, their eyes, their movements, reading them for potential threat. The dizziness would return without warning, often when he was reading a manuscript and a name on the page matched the cadence of the guards’ voices, the reminder striking him just as sharply as the sound in the facility. He would close his eyes, wait for the floor to steady, and keep reading. For months, he had managed the startle responses, the undereating, the careful distance from old friends, and the relentless questioning of how it could have been different. He would try to deliberately recall the hours in the facility, but the memories slipped past like water through cupped hands, leaving him with fragments, a raised hand, a shouted name, the taste of copper, while larger stretches simply vanished. The story of his torture felt so extreme that he was certain it belonged to someone else, yet the gaps in his recall were not a failure of effort but a persistent absence. The divorce had been amicable, but it had left him with a house that felt too large and a routine that had hardened into habit. He had come to therapy now because he wanted to understand the parts of his own story that remained out of reach and because he was tired of living in a state of quiet readiness. He is most afraid that the past will keep folding into the present, that the narrative of his torture will eventually feel as impossible to voice as it does when he tries to speak of it, but he hopes that someone might help him find the words to hold it without letting it hold him.
